# Results — Study 957 (Holdco Discount) on the real daily tape

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Seven listed holding companies
whose value is dominated by one **listed** stake, so NAV can be marked from the tape:
`discount = 1 - P_holdco / (k * P_stake + other)`, built from **price-only**
(split-adjusted, dividend-unadjusted) closes. Every **return** comes from **total-return**
closes (`yfinance`, `auto_adjust=True`). The tests use the **trailing z** of the discount —
each name standardised against its own preceding 504 days — because the *level* of every
series is only as good as the `k` / `other` assumptions in
[docs/references.md](references.md). One execution lag throughout: the z formed through the
close of day t sets the position held over day t+1. Panel window 2004-01-02 → 2026-06-30.
As-of **2026-06-30** (the partial current month is dropped).*

## Data stamp

| Legs | Window | Holdcos | Fingerprint |
|---|---|---|---|
| 7 holdco/stake pairs + `^IRX` cash proxy | 2004-01-02 → 2026-06-30 | 7 | Fingerprint `d51337b2a3bb` |

## The panel

| Holdco | Stake | n days | Window | Discount mean | sd | AR(1) half-life |
|---|---|--:|---|--:|--:|--:|
| Heineken Holding | Heineken NV | 5,680 | 2004-05 → 2026-06 | +11.7% | 4.2% | 95 d |
| Christian Dior | LVMH | 5,762 | 2004-01 → 2026-06 | +14.7% | 9.1% | 232 d |
| Liberty Broadband | Charter | 2,522 | 2014-11 → 2024-11 | +6.2% | 19.4% | 184 d |
| Naspers | Tencent | 4,146 | 2010-01 → 2026-06 | +37.9% | 19.5% | 329 d |
| Prosus | Tencent | 1,596 | 2020-02 → 2026-06 | +36.3% | 7.7% | 94 d |
| Bollore | Vivendi | 5,362 | 2004-01 → 2024-11 | +74.4% | 13.7% | 1,514 d |
| SoftBank | Alibaba | 1,835 | 2014-09 → 2021-12 | +59.9% | 8.7% | 105 d |

Three names are truncated, all on **corporate events announced in advance**, never on
performance, and all three *shorten* the sample: Bollore at the December 2024 Vivendi
four-way split, SoftBank at the 2022 Alibaba disposal, and Liberty Broadband at the
2024-11-13 Charter merger agreement — after which its gap is a **merger spread** with a
contractual exchange ratio, i.e. Study 366's subject and not a holdco discount. That last cut
removes the one window in the whole panel where convergence was *guaranteed*, so keeping it
would have been the generous choice; the sensitivity is reported at the bottom of this page.

## (a) Does the discount mean-revert?

Forward 126-day change in the discount regressed on today's trailing z. **Negative beta =
a wide gap narrows.**

| Holdco | n | beta | HAC *t* | R² |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Heineken Holding | 5,303 | −0.0024 | −0.83 | 0.010 |
| Christian Dior | 5,539 | **+0.0037** | +0.76 | 0.009 |
| Liberty Broadband | 2,145 | −0.0031 | −0.44 | 0.002 |
| Naspers | 3,769 | −0.0069 | −1.12 | 0.018 |
| Prosus | 1,219 | −0.0358 | **−4.07** | 0.362 |
| Bollore | 5,139 | **+0.0031** | +1.01 | 0.011 |
| SoftBank | 1,458 | −0.0208 | −1.82 | 0.088 |
| **POOLED (Driscoll-Kraay)** | **24,572 over 5,581 days** | **−0.0002** | **−0.09** | 0.0000 |

**The answer is no.** The pooled slope is the right sign and utterly invisible: *t* = −0.09,
R² = 0.0000. Knowing that a holdco's discount is a standard deviation wider than its own
two-year average tells you **nothing** about where the gap will be six months later. The sign
is negative in **5 of 7** names, which is what a coin flip looks like, and the one strongly
significant result — Prosus, *t* = −4.07 — sits on the shortest sample in the panel (1,219
usable days), where a 504-day trailing window and a 126-day forward window overlap so heavily
that a handful of independent episodes carry the whole regression. Two names (Christian Dior,
Bollore) have the **wrong** sign: a wide gap got wider.

The horizon is a convention rather than a result: at h = 21 the pooled slope is −0.0006
(*t* = −1.18), at h = 63 −0.0006 (*t* = −0.40), at h = 252 +0.0011 (*t* = +0.30). Nothing
clears anywhere.

Half-lives say the same thing more plainly. Bollore's discount has an AR(1) half-life of
**1,514 trading days** — six years. It went from 46% to 96% and never came back.

## (b) Does buying the wide discount pay?

The tradable expression is the **dollar-neutral pair**: long the holdco, short the stake one
for one. That ratio is not a choice — since `P_holdco = (1 − d) · k · P_stake`, a
dollar-neutral long/short earns exactly the change in `log(1 − d)` and nothing else. The
timed arm holds a name only while its z ≥ 1 (entered) until z ≤ 0 (exited); the always-on
arm holds every available name every day. Both are long/short pairs funded from collateral,
so **both are excess-of-cash by construction**. Costs 10 bps one-way per leg; borrow 100
bps/yr on the short leg.

| Arm | Net Sharpe | CAGR | Vol | Max DD | HAC *t* | Gross Sharpe | Gross *t* | Invested |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **Timed (wide discount)** | **+0.312** | +2.01% | 7.2% | −17.9% | **+1.69** | **+0.566** | **+3.04** | 80.7% |
| Always-on (no timing) | −0.268 | −1.68% | 5.7% | −43.8% | −1.41 | +0.046 | +0.24 | 100% |

Timing advantage +0.580, HAC *t* on the daily difference **+3.25**. So on the full panel the
gross number *does* clear the bar — and the next four tables are why it should not be
believed.

### Bootstrap Sharpe CIs (2,000 draws, 21-day blocks)

| Arm | Sharpe | 95% CI | share < 0 |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| Timed, **net** | +0.312 | **[−0.050, +0.656]** | 4.7% |
| Timed, gross | +0.566 | [+0.204, +0.910] | 0.1% |
| Always-on, net | −0.268 | [−0.645, +0.093] | 93.0% |

The net CI includes zero. The whole result lives in the gap between gross and net.

### Cost and borrow sweeps

| One-way cost | Timed Sharpe (*t*) | | Borrow | Timed Sharpe (*t*) |
|---|--:|---|---|--:|
| 0 bps | +0.510 (+2.75) | | 0 bps | +0.367 (+1.99) |
| 5 bps | +0.411 (+2.22) | | 100 bps | +0.312 (+1.69) |
| **10 bps** | **+0.312 (+1.69)** | | 300 bps | +0.202 (+1.09) |
| 25 bps | +0.016 (+0.08) | | 600 bps | +0.036 (+0.20) |
| 50 bps | −0.467 (−2.52) | | | |

The edge is gone at 25 bps one-way and negative at 50. This is a two-legged trade in names
including two OTC ADRs and a Paris small-cap; 10 bps is the *optimistic* end.

### The rule's own free parameters

`enter = 1.0` / `exit = 0.0` in trailing-z units are the only genuinely free parameters in
the design, and an unswept free parameter is a hidden choice. The whole grid, not the
reported cell:

| enter \ exit | −0.50 | 0.00 | +0.50 |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| **0.50** | +0.275 (+1.56) | +0.463 (+2.61) | — |
| **0.75** | +0.306 (+1.73) | +0.489 (+2.72) | +0.629 (+3.36) |
| **1.00** | +0.399 (+2.22) | **+0.566 (+3.04)** | +0.653 (+3.43) |
| **1.25** | +0.377 (+2.06) | +0.480 (+2.56) | +0.508 (+2.67) |
| **1.50** | +0.402 (+2.20) | +0.455 (+2.47) | +0.472 (+2.46) |
| **2.00** | +0.338 (+1.90) | +0.384 (+2.13) | +0.301 (+1.66) |

*(gross Sharpe and gross HAC t; cells with exit ≥ enter are skipped as having no hysteresis
band. The bold cell is the headline.)*

Two things to take from it, one in each direction. The headline is **not** the best cell —
enter 1.0 / exit +0.5 is better (+0.653, *t* = +3.43) and so is enter 0.75 / exit +0.5 — so
the reported number is not the top of a mined grid. But **no cell in the grid produces a net
*t* of 2**: across all 17, net *t* runs from +0.08 to +1.90 and gross *t* from +1.56 to
+3.43. There is no threshold pair at which this trade is significant after friction.

### The standardisation window

504 days was a convention. It is also, as it turns out, the best of the five:

| Trailing window | Gross Sharpe (*t*) | Net Sharpe (*t*) | Pooled MR beta (*t*) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 252 d | +0.446 (+2.42) | +0.152 (+0.83) | −0.0010 (−0.37) |
| 378 d | +0.455 (+2.46) | +0.195 (+1.06) | −0.0003 (−0.12) |
| **504 d** | **+0.566 (+3.04)** | **+0.312 (+1.69)** | −0.0002 (−0.09) |
| 756 d | +0.333 (+1.89) | +0.112 (+0.63) | +0.0004 (+0.16) |
| 1008 d | +0.160 (+0.94) | −0.054 (−0.32) | +0.0002 (+0.09) |

This is stated because it is the least flattering table on the page. The headline sits at the
**maximum** of the window sweep; move the standardisation to four years and the gross *t*
falls to +0.94. The mean-reversion answer is flat everywhere, so nothing about conclusion (a)
turns on it — but the gross trading number, already the weaker half of the case, is worth
about a point of *t* less at any other window than the one that was chosen.

### The check that decides it — stale quotes

Four of the seven pairs are primary-exchange listings where both legs print in the same
liquid session (Heineken Holding, Christian Dior, Liberty Broadband, Bollore). The other
three are **thin OTC ADRs** (NPSNY, PROSY, SFTBY), whose closes can be hours old or simply
not refreshed — and a stale close on one leg of a long/short pair manufactures exactly the
pattern this study is looking for: an apparent gap that "reverts" tomorrow when the quote
catches up.

| Sub-panel | Timed net Sharpe (*t*) | Timed gross Sharpe (*t*) |
|---|--:|--:|
| Primary listings only (4 names) | +0.148 (**+0.76**) | +0.368 (**+1.87**) |
| The 3 OTC ADR pairs alone | +0.389 (+1.85) | +0.458 (+2.16) |

Strip the stale-quote names and the gross *t* falls from **+3.04 to +1.87**, the net *t* to
**+0.76**. The pooled mean-reversion slope on the clean four is +0.0033 (*t* = +1.27) —
the wrong sign.

### Everything else, for completeness

- **Per name, standalone:** not one of the seven clears |*t*| = 2 on its own. Best are
  Prosus (+0.66, *t* = +1.61) and SoftBank (+0.40, *t* = +1.17) — the two thinnest ADRs.
  Heineken Holding +0.15, Christian Dior +0.09, Liberty Broadband +0.07, Bollore +0.09.
- **Era cut (2016):** timed +0.319 (*t* = +1.33) early, +0.256 (*t* = +0.86) late. Same sign
  both halves, significant in neither.
- **Leave-one-out:** timed net Sharpe stays in +0.26 … +0.35 (*t* +1.41 … +1.87) whichever
  name is dropped. Nothing here is one holdco wearing a panel costume — and nothing here
  reaches |*t*| = 2 either.
- **NAV-calibration sweep:** `k` from 0.8× to 1.2× and the `other` term from 0.5× to 1.5×
  move the timed Sharpe only between +0.275 and +0.321, and the pooled mean-reversion *t*
  stays inside ±0.3 throughout. The verdict is not an artefact of the assumption table —
  which is exactly what the trailing-z design was built to guarantee. (For the four names
  whose `other` term is zero, `k` cancels out of a z-score **exactly**, so the anchoring of
  `k` to a reported discount cannot leak hindsight into any test.)
- **Hedge construction:** shorting the whole look-through stake value instead of hedging
  dollar-for-dollar turns the timed arm negative (net −0.040, *t* = −0.24). That variant
  over-hedges a proportional gap and leaves the pair net short the underlying through a
  22-year equity bull market, so its number is about beta, not about discounts — but it is a
  fair reminder of how construction-sensitive this corner is.
- **Long-only, excess-of-cash:** owning the holdcos only when their discount is wide earns
  +0.536 excess Sharpe against +0.655 for simply owning them all the time and +0.636 for
  owning the stakes instead (HAC *t* on the difference **+0.02**). Unhedged, the timing adds
  exactly nothing.
- **Cash-leg cross-check:** the `^IRX` proxy compounds to 1.45%/yr against BIL's actual
  1.36%/yr total return over BIL's window — close enough that the excess-of-cash race does
  not turn on it.
- **The Liberty Broadband truncation, both ways:** running LBRDK/CHTR to the as-of date
  instead (i.e. keeping the 406 days of live merger spread) leaves the timed pair identical
  to three decimals (net +0.312, gross +0.566) and moves the pooled mean-reversion slope to
  +0.0005 (*t* = +0.19), right sign in 4/7 rather than 5/7. Either way the answer to (a) is a
  *t* of essentially zero; the cut is made because a contractual convergence is a different
  trade, not because it changes the result.
- **Synthetic control** (machinery proof only, never supports the stamp): on a *planted*
  Ornstein-Uhlenbeck discount the pooled regression fires hard (mean *t* = **−11.8**, 4/4
  seeds) and the timed rule earns a gross Sharpe of **+1.00**; on the martingale null the
  pooled *t* averages **−0.38** and the gross Sharpe **+0.13**. The detector finds real
  reversion when it is there and is quiet when it is not — so the flat real-tape answer is a
  property of holdcos, not of the harness.

## Verdict

- **Signal — Weak.** The load-bearing half of the thesis is simply absent: a discount one
  standard deviation wider than its own two-year average predicts **nothing** about the gap
  six months later (pooled Driscoll-Kraay *t* = **−0.09**, R² = 0.0000, sign negative in 5/7
  names, which is a coin flip, and two names where the wide gap got wider). The trading half
  looks better at first — gross Sharpe **+0.566**, HAC *t* = **+3.04** — but it does not
  survive any of the three checks that matter. Charge realistic friction and it falls to
  *t* = +1.69, with a bootstrap CI that includes zero and nothing left at 25 bps. Remove the
  three thin OTC ADR pairs, whose stale closes manufacture precisely this pattern in a
  long/short book, and the gross *t* falls to **+1.87** and the net to **+0.76**. Sweep the
  two thresholds that define the rule and **not one of the 17 cells reaches a net *t* of
  2**; sweep the standardisation window and the headline turns out to be the best of five.
  No single name clears |*t*| = 2 standalone, and neither era does. What is left is a faint,
  friction-sized reversal in the least liquid corner of the panel — enough to be interesting,
  nowhere near enough to be an edge.
- **Tradability — Mirage.** The net bootstrap CI is [−0.050, +0.656]; the strategy is flat at
  25 bps one-way and −0.47 Sharpe at 50; it needs a short leg in the very OTC ADRs that are
  producing the number; and it reverses sign entirely under the other defensible hedge
  construction. The always-on version — just owning the discount and waiting — lost money
  (−0.268 Sharpe, CAGR −1.68%) over 22 years. Buying a conglomerate below the sum of its
  parts bought a *cheaper* conglomerate, not a closing gap.
- **What the discount actually is.** Every persistent explanation of it — dividend tax
  leakage up the chain, a control block that makes takeover impossible, holding-company
  overhead, the risk that management reinvests your capital badly — is a story about a
  *price*, not an *error*. Prices of control have no reason to converge on your timetable,
  and Bollore's six-year half-life is what that looks like on a chart.
